# Proteinuria

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Basics of nephrology > Proteinuria*

[Original Article Link](/library/0Q0euf)

---

## Summary

Proteinuria is defined as a urinary protein excretion of > 150 mg/24 h. It has many possible causes, which may be benign (e.g., <u>fever</u>, intense exercise, <u>dehydration</u>) or more serious (e.g., <u>glomerulonephritis</u>, <u>multiple myeloma</u>). There are three different pathophysiological mechanisms that may lead to proteinuria: damage to the <u>glomeruli</u> (<u>glomerular</u>), damage to the tubules (tubular), or overproduction of low-molecular-weight <u>proteins</u> (overflow). If proteinuria is detected, patients should be further evaluated (e.g., additional urinalyses) to determine the underlying cause. The detection of <u>microalbuminuria</u> is of particular importance, as it suggests early diabetic or <u>hypertensive nephropathy</u>.

---

## Definition

Proteinuria = urinary protein excretion of > 150 mg/24 h

---

## Diagnosis

### <u>Urinalysis</u>




* <u>Urine dipstick</u>: repeat to rule out <u>transient proteinuria</u> (primarily detects <u>albumin</u>)

* Sulfosalicylic acid test: sulfosalicylic acid is added to urine to measure total urine <u>proteins</u> (not specific for <u>albumin</u>)

* 24-hour urine collection or urine protein-to-<u>creatinine</u> <u>ratio</u> in a <u>spot urine</u> sample to rule out <u>orthostatic proteinuria</u>

* <u>Urine sediment</u> to rule out <u>glomerular disease</u>

* <u>Electrophoresis</u>;   to rule out <u>tubulointerstitial diseases</u> and <u>multiple myeloma</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Proteinuria can cause foamy urine.




### Diagnosis of underlying disease




* See “<u>Differential diagnoses of nephrotic syndrome</u>.”

* See “<u>Diabetes mellitus</u>.”

* See “<u>Multiple myeloma</u>.”

## Classification

### According to quantity




#### Moderately increased albuminuria (formerly <u>microalbuminuria</u>)




* Urine <u>albumin</u> excretion of 30–300 mg/24 h

* Diagnosis is made if two out of three tests are positive.

* Early symptom of <u>diabetic nephropathy</u> and <u>hypertensive nephropathy</u>

* Specific <u>urine dipstick</u> tests; , radioimmunoassay, or <u>ELISA</u> required for detection





#### Severely increased albuminuria (formerly <u>macroalbuminuria</u>)




* Urine <u>albumin</u> excretion > 300 mg/24 h

* Standard <u>urine dipstick</u> tests can be used for detection.

* <u>Nephrotic syndrome</u>: massive proteinuria (> 3.5 g/24 h), <u>hypoalbuminemia</u>, <u>edema</u>, and <u>hyperlipidemia</u>





### According to origin




#### Glomerular proteinuria [[2]](/library/59aiL5)[[3]](/library/M9aML5)




* Damage to the <u>glomeruli</u> → increased permeability of the <u>glomerular filtration barrier</u> → urinary protein excretion

* Characteristic finding: appearance of large <u>proteins</u> in the urine

* Selective glomerular proteinuria 

* Loss of negative charge of <u>glomerular basement membrane</u>

* Only small- to medium-sized <u>proteins</u> can be found in the urine (primarily <u>albumin</u>)

* Can be found in diseases with mild damage to the <u>glomeruli</u> (e.g., <u>minimal change disease</u>, <u>IgA nephropathy</u>)

* Non-selective glomerular proteinuria

* Damage to the <u>glomerular basement membrane</u>

* All types of protein of any size can be found in the urine (<u>albumin</u>, <u>transferrin</u>, and <u>IgG</u> are commonly detected)

* Can be found in diseases with severe damage to the <u>glomeruli</u> and subsequent permeability to all components of the blood (e.g., <u>rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis</u>, <u>lupus nephritis</u>, <u>amyloid nephropathy</u>)





#### Tubular proteinuria




* Damage to the tubules → failure to reabsorb small <u>proteins</u> in the tubules → urinary protein excretion

* The detection of <u>beta-2 microglobulin</u> without large <u>proteins</u> is typical.

* Can be found in <u>tubulointerstitial nephritis</u>, <u>analgesics</u> nephropathy, <u>acute renal failure</u>





#### Mixed proteinuria



* Found in diseases that affect both the <u>glomeruli</u> and the tubules (e.g., <u>chronic renal failure</u>)




#### Prerenal proteinuria (or <u>overflow proteinuria</u>)



* Increased production of low-molecular-weight <u>proteins</u> → The reabsorption capacity of the tubules is exceeded.

* <u>Light chains</u> or <u>Bence-Jones protein</u> (see <u>myeloma kidney</u>)

* <u>Hemoglobinuria</u> (in <u>hemolysis</u>)

* <u>Myoglobinuria</u> (in <u>rhabdomyolysis</u>)




#### Postrenal proteinuria




* <u>Proteins</u> that are being produced in the tubules (Tamm-Horsfall protein)

* <u>Proteins</u> that reach the urine in the <u>lower urinary tract</u> (e.g., trauma or inflammation)

---

## Benign proteinuria

* Defined as isolated proteinuria < 3.5 g/24 h

* Important, benign differential diagnosis in the evaluation of proteinuria

* Very common; mostly affects younger individuals

* Types of <u>benign proteinuria</u>

* Orthostatic proteinuria (<u>postural proteinuria</u>): increased protein excretion only in the upright position

* Transient proteinuria

* Most common cause of isolated proteinuria in children

* Causes:

* Heavy exertion/<u>stress</u>

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Seizures</u>

* Exposure to cold temperatures

* Women can present with mild proteinuria due to <u>vaginal discharge</u>.

* A <u>dipstick test</u> should be repeated to exclude underlying disease.

* No treatment necessary; excellent prognosis
